rules.statement: Don't report an `async ValueTask` method just because its common path usually completes synchronously; only ask for a hand-written fast path when a measured cost shows it is needed.
rules.why: An async ValueTask state machine is a struct that is boxed only when an await doesn't complete at once, so the synchronous path allocates nothing, and without a measured cost the simpler async form stays.
rules.check: Before flagging an async method for the async seam on a mostly-synchronous path, check whether it returns ValueTask, whether the awaited calls usually complete synchronously, and whether any benchmark shows a cost.

rules.statement: Don't report a private async helper that returns `Task` instead of `ValueTask` when its result is discarded by a callback API such as `SynchronizationContext.Post` and a comment records why.
rules.why: A ValueTask must be consumed exactly once (CA2012), so a discarded ValueTask would break that rule; returning ValueTask and calling `.AsTask()` would only add a conversion.
rules.check: Look at whether the helper's result is discarded by its caller (posted callbacks, fire-and-forget with errors routed elsewhere) and whether a comment above it records the exception to the ValueTask convention.

rules.statement: Don't report the parameter count of an overload family (such as arity 1 to 8 state overloads) that deliberately mirrors an existing sibling API's overloads.
rules.why: Keeping parallel factories (for example sync and async) in step is the intent, and capping arity or using a single state type would make them differ.
rules.check: Before flagging many-parameter overloads, check whether a sibling type already ships the same overload set and whether an ADR records the parity.

rules.statement: Don't report an optional trailing `CancellationToken cancellationToken = default` on a method that mirrors a BCL method with the same optional token and has a single overload.
rules.why: A trailing token is what the convention asks for; making it required would force every caller without one to pass `CancellationToken.None`, and the one-overload-with-optional-parameters rule still holds.
rules.check: Check whether the token is trailing, whether the wrapped BCL API (e.g. `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync`) and the sync sibling take it optionally, and whether there is only one overload.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't report randomized `Task.Run` race tests as not proving overlap when gated deterministic tests beside them already cover the interleaving and the race tests are kept as stress tests.
rules.why: The randomized tests are a deliberate extra check; a start barrier would make overlap more likely without proving it, and the gated tests are the ones that cover the window.
rules.check: Look for sibling gated tests (TaskCompletionSource or ManualResetEventSlim holding an operation open) covering the same interleaving before flagging a race test.

rules.statement: In a test project, test a concurrency window deterministically by gating one operation open (a `TaskCompletionSource` for async, a bounded `ManualResetEventSlim` for sync), running the competing operation, asserting the intermediate state, then releasing the gate.
rules.why: Unsynchronized `Task.Run` loops with mocks that complete immediately may never hit the interleaving, so a regression there goes unnoticed.
rules.check: For thread-safe types with CAS or lock-free state machines (set vs dispose, release vs dispose, add vs dispose), check that at least one gated test holds the window open; flag suites with only single-threaded or ungated race tests.

rules.statement: In a test project, make an async delegate stub fail by returning a faulted task (`ValueTask.FromException(...)`/`Task.FromException(...)`) rather than throwing synchronously with `() => throw ...`.
rules.why: A synchronously throwing stub doesn't cover an awaited task that faults, which is how real async code fails.
rules.check: Look for `Func<ValueTask>` or `Func<Task>` stubs written as `() => throw ...` in tests of failure paths.

rules.statement: In a test project, assert the exact expected exception type (and inner exceptions where relevant) instead of `Assert.ThrowsAny<Exception>`/`ThrowsAnyAsync<Exception>`.
rules.why: Accepting any exception lets an unrelated one, such as an ObjectDisposedException, keep the test green.
rules.check: Flag `ThrowsAny<Exception>` / `ThrowsAnyAsync<Exception>` and compare with the sync twin test's assertions.

rules.statement: In a test project, a null-argument test captures the `ArgumentNullException` and asserts its `ParamName`.
rules.why: A null check that names the wrong parameter would otherwise still pass.
rules.check: Look for bare `Assert.Throws<ArgumentNullException>(...)` without a following `ParamName` assertion.

rules.statement: In a test project, give every public method that guards a null argument its own null-argument test, including each sibling overload or extension method.
rules.why: If one guard were dropped or named the wrong parameter, callers would get a NullReferenceException or wrong ParamName and the suite would stay green.
rules.check: Compare the set of public methods with `ArgumentNullException` guards against the null-argument tests; flag siblings (e.g. WriteLock next to ReadLock) with none.

rules.statement: In a test project, a test that checks something does not throw must assert it explicitly, e.g. `Assert.Null(Record.Exception(...))` or `Record.ExceptionAsync`, not just call the code or discard a read.
rules.why: A test with no assertion shows nothing explicit, and a cleanup could delete an apparently unused read, leaving a test that asserts nothing.
rules.check: Flag tests with no Assert/Verify call, or ending in a bare discard like `_ = x.Property;` used as an implicit check.

rules.statement: In a test project, each test asserts one behavior; split a test whose name or assertions cover two behaviors (e.g. `..._PropagatesAndDisposes...`) into one test per behavior.
rules.why: When one test checks two behaviors, a failure doesn't show which behavior broke.
rules.check: Look for test names joining two outcomes with And, or tests asserting unrelated outcomes.

rules.statement: Keep README prose consistent with the sample it introduces, and when README samples are generated from tests (e.g. mdsnippets), fix the source test and regenerate rather than editing the README.
rules.why: Prose that describes a different type than the sample shows leaves readers unable to tell which behavior applies, and hand edits to generated snippets are lost.
rules.check: Compare each README lead-in sentence to the types and calls in the snippet below it; check that snippet changes come from the test file.

rules.statement: A code comment describes the synchronization the code actually uses and sits on the member or accessor that does it.
rules.why: Comments copied from elsewhere (e.g. naming SpinLock above a CompareExchange loop) or placed above a getter that only reads mislead readers about the primitive and the behavior.
rules.check: Compare comments about locking or retry loops with the code directly below them; flag comments above `get` that describe `set` behavior.

rules.statement: Don't name a member the same as a commonly used type it's next to, such as a property `Action` of type `Action<T>`; use a role name like `Callback`.
rules.why: The property and the type are easy to confuse when reading the code.
rules.check: Look for members named `Action`, `Func`, `Task` or other BCL type names, especially when typed as that type.

rules.statement: Write an ADR's Context section in present terms that stay true after the decision is applied, not as a description of the code before the change.
rules.why: After merge a Context describing the old state contradicts both the Decision and the code.
rules.check: In changed ADRs, look for Context sentences describing current code that the change itself makes false.

rules.statement: When a change adds public overloads or static state, update the architecture docs that list the API surface or claim what static state exists.
rules.why: Otherwise readers of the component table miss the new overloads and the doc gives a wrong picture of static state.
rules.check: For new public overloads or static fields and delegates, check docs/architecture.md (or equivalent) tables and statements about static state.

rules.statement: When code calls `SynchronizationContext.OperationStarted()` before `Post`, call `OperationCompleted()` and rethrow if `Post` throws.
rules.why: Otherwise a context that rejects the post leaves its operation count unbalanced and the failure is silent.
rules.check: Look for OperationStarted followed by Post without a try/catch that balances with OperationCompleted on failure.
